planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained soil along shady trail edges or canyon slopes; seed can also be sown and cold-stratified over winter but germination is slow and uneven.

directions: Canyon gooseberry is a spiny, open-arching California native shrub that does best in light to partial shade along woodland edges and canyon slopes rather than in exposed full sun. Maroon-and-white, fuchsia-like flowers appear in late winter and early spring and are an early hummingbird draw, followed by bristly purple-red berries that are edible once the spines are rubbed or peeled away. It is drought tolerant once established, especially near the coast, and provides significant cover and food value for birds. Avoid heavy summer irrigation in hot inland gardens, where root rot can become an issue in poorly drained soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or root cuttings in fall as the rainy season begins, siting in the dry shade or part shade of oaks and other established trees; little to no summer water is needed once roots are established.

directions: Chaparral currant is unusual among fruiting shrubs for tolerating full shade as well as part shade, making it a good understory choice beneath coast live oak and other California natives. Pink to deep red flower clusters open in the dead of winter, well before most garden plants, and are an important early nectar source for migrating hummingbirds. The small, dark purple-black berries that follow in late spring are edible, though they are seedy and more valued by wildlife than for fresh eating. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and generally needs no supplemental water beyond winter rainfall in the right site.

planting.note: Plant container stock or root cuttings in fall in well-drained soil on the shaded north side of a structure or beneath open pine canopy; seed needs a cold winter stratification period if starting from seed instead.

directions: Sierra gooseberry is a compact, spiny mountain shrub native to open pine forest and chaparral slopes of the Sierra Nevada and northern California, where it grows well in the moist part shade found under tree canopy. The round berries ripen from green to red-purple and are enclosed in a soft spiny husk; peeling back this layer reveals a tasty fruit good for fresh eating or gooseberry jam. Its naturally compact size makes it easier to fit into a shaded border than many other native Ribes species. It tolerates dry, open forest conditions well once established but appreciates occasional water during its first couple of seasons.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall at the start of the rainy season, choosing a part-shade site such as a north- or east-facing slope or beneath oak canopy; established plants need little to no summer irrigation.

directions: White-flowering currant is a Southern California chaparral native often found growing in the dappled shade of large oaks or along seasonal creek banks, and it performs best in a garden site that mimics those conditions. Fragrant white flower sprays, with a scent reminiscent of vanilla or clove, open in winter and early spring ahead of most other shrubs. The small, hairy, sticky berries that follow range from orange to purple or red and are edible, though they are more important as wildlife food than as a table fruit. It is extremely drought tolerant once established, making it a good low-water choice for dry shade under established trees.
